## Why GLMs in ecology {#sec-why-glm}

Counts are not normal, proportions live in $[0,1]$, presences are binary. The Gaussian
linear model treats all of them as if they were continuous and unbounded, and fails in
predictable ways: confidence intervals that include negative richness, misspecified
variance, fan-shaped residuals.

The GLM fixes this with two choices: the **distribution** of the response and the
**link function** connecting the mean to the linear predictor.

| Response | Distribution | Link | In Julia |
|---|---|---|---|
| Count | Poisson | log | `Poisson(), LogLink()` |
| Overdispersed count | Negative binomial | log | `negbin(...)` |
| Presence/absence | Bernoulli/Binomial | logit | `Binomial(), LogitLink()` |
| Proportion with denominator | Binomial | logit | `Binomial(), LogitLink()` |
| Positive skewed continuous | Gamma | log | `Gamma(), LogLink()` |

## Poisson: species richness {#sec-poisson}

```{julia}
#| label: glm-poisson
g1 = glm(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c),
         ponds, Poisson(), LogLink())
```

The generating process used
$\log\mu = 0.9 + 0.28\log(\text{area}) - 0.011\,\text{canopy} + 0.03\,(\text{temp}-24.5) + \dots$

```{julia}
#| label: poisson-truth
DataFrame(
    term      = coefnames(g1),
    estimated = round.(coef(g1), digits = 4),
    truth     = [missing, 0.28, -0.011, 0.03],
)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 9.1 — Adding hydroperiod

Fit a Poisson GLM like `g1`, adding `hydro` at the end of the formula. Pass its
coefficients to `check("9.1", ...)`, then compare its AIC with that of `g1`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Copy `g1` and add `+ hydro`. `aic(g)` gives the AIC; lower is better.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-1
g_hydro = glm(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c + hydro),
              ponds, Poisson(), LogLink())
coef(g_hydro)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-1-check
check("9.1", coef(g_hydro))
(aic_g1 = aic(g1), aic_hydro = aic(g_hydro))
```

The AIC drops by about 9, so `hydro` earns its place. The simulation added 0.22 to
the log mean of permanent ponds; the model estimates −0.19 for temporary ones, the same
effect seen from the other side.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-9-1
#| include: false
Checks.verify("9.1", coef(g_hydro))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Interpreting coefficients on the log scale

A coefficient $\beta$ under a log link means that a one-unit increase in the predictor
multiplies the mean by $e^\beta$. For `canopy`:

```{julia}
#| label: interpretation
exp(coef(g1)[3]), (exp(coef(g1)[3]) - 1) * 100
```

That is, each additional percentage point of canopy reduces expected richness by about
1%.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 9.2 — Temporary ponds, in plain numbers

Using the model from 9.1, by what factor does expected richness change in a temporary
pond compared with a permanent one, all else equal? Pass that factor to
`check("9.2", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

The `hydro: temporary` coefficient is the fifth. Under a log link, a coefficient
$\beta$ multiplies the mean by $e^\beta$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-2
factor_temp = exp(coef(g_hydro)[5])
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-2-check
check("9.2", factor_temp)
```

About 0.83: temporary ponds are expected to hold about 17% fewer species than
permanent ones.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-9-2
#| include: false
Checks.verify("9.2", factor_temp)
```

## Overdispersion {#sec-overdispersion}

The Poisson assumes $\text{Var}(Y) = \text{E}(Y)$. Ecological data rarely cooperate.

```{julia}
#| label: dispersion
# Pearson residual: (y - mu) / sqrt(Var(mu)). For the Poisson, Var(mu) = mu.
mu = predict(g1)
pearson_res = (ponds.richness .- mu) ./ sqrt.(mu)
df_res = dof_residual(g1)
phi = sum(pearson_res .^ 2) / df_res

(dispersion_statistic = phi,
 verdict = phi > 1.5 ? "overdispersed" : "acceptable")
```

If $\hat\phi \gg 1$, the alternatives are the negative binomial or a mixed model with
an observation-level random effect.

::: {.callout-important}
## Overdispersion is a symptom, not a diagnosis

`ponds.csv` was generated as a *pure* Poisson process — there is no extra-Poisson
variance in the data-generating code. Yet $\hat\phi \approx 1.95$. Why?

Because the generating model included a region effect that `g1` omits. Unmodelled
heterogeneity inflates the dispersion statistic exactly as genuine overdispersion
does, and the statistic cannot tell you which one you have.

This matters practically: the reflex of reaching for a negative binomial whenever
$\hat\phi > 1.5$ can paper over a missing predictor. Check your model structure
before you change your distribution. The GLMM in @sec-glmm addresses the actual cause
here.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 9.3 — Testing the warning

The box above claims that the overdispersion of `g1` comes from a missing predictor.
Test it: fit a Poisson GLM with `log_area`, `canopy`, `temp_c`, `hydro` and `region`,
compute its dispersion statistic as in the block above, and pass it to
`check("9.3", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Copy the dispersion block, replacing `g1` with your model. `predict(g)` gives the
fitted means.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-3
g_full = glm(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c + hydro + region),
             ponds, Poisson(), LogLink())

mu_full = predict(g_full)
phi_full = sum(((ponds.richness .- mu_full) ./ sqrt.(mu_full)) .^ 2) /
           dof_residual(g_full)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-3-check
check("9.3", phi_full)
```

About 0.94: with the predictors of the generating model in place, the
"overdispersion" is gone. Adding `hydro` alone (9.1) barely moved it; `region` was the
missing piece.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-9-3
#| include: false
Checks.verify("9.3", phi_full)
```

```{julia}
#| label: negbin
g2 = negbin(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c), ponds, LogLink())
```

```{julia}
#| label: poisson-vs-nb
DataFrame(
    model  = ["Poisson", "Negative binomial"],
    aic    = round.([aic(g1), aic(g2)], digits = 1),
    bic    = round.([bic(g1), bic(g2)], digits = 1),
    loglik = round.([loglikelihood(g1), loglikelihood(g2)], digits = 1),
)
```

## Offsets {#sec-offset}

When sampling effort varies across units, model the **rate** rather than the raw
count, using an offset.

```{julia}
#| label: offset
g3 = glm(@formula(richness ~ canopy + temp_c), ponds, Poisson(), LogLink();
         offset = log.(ponds.area_m2))

coeftable(g3)
```

This models richness *per unit area*, fixing the `log(area)` coefficient at 1.

## Logistic regression {#sec-logistic}

```{julia}
#| label: glm-logistic
g4 = glm(@formula(focal ~ canopy + temp_c + hydro),
         ponds, Binomial(), LogitLink())
```

```{julia}
#| label: odds-ratios
DataFrame(
    term       = coefnames(g4),
    coef       = round.(coef(g4), digits = 4),
    odds_ratio = round.(exp.(coef(g4)), digits = 3),
    ci_lower   = round.(exp.(confint(g4)[:, 1]), digits = 3),
    ci_upper   = round.(exp.(confint(g4)[:, 2]), digits = 3),
)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 9.4 — Odds for a meaningful change

The odds ratio for one percentage point of canopy is close to 1, which is hard to
interpret. Compute the odds ratio for an increase of **10** percentage points, from
`g4`, and pass it to `check("9.4", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Ten points multiply the odds by $e^{10\beta}$, not by $10\,e^{\beta}$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-4
or_10 = exp(10 * coef(g4)[2])
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-4-check
check("9.4", or_10)
```

About 1.19: each extra 10 points of canopy multiply the odds of finding the focal
species by 1.19, an increase of 19%.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-9-4
#| include: false
Checks.verify("9.4", or_10)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-logistic
#| fig-cap: "Predicted probability of focal-species occurrence along the canopy gradient."
grid = DataFrame(
    canopy = repeat(range(0, 100, length = 100), 2),
    temp_c = fill(mean(ponds.temp_c), 200),
    hydro  = repeat(["permanent", "temporary"], inner = 100),
)
grid.p = predict(g4, grid)

fig = Figure(size = (700, 430))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Canopy cover (%)",
          ylabel = "P(occurrence)", title = "Focal species")

for (h, col) in zip(["permanent", "temporary"], [:steelblue, :darkorange])
    sub = grid[grid.hydro .== h, :]
    lines!(ax, sub.canopy, sub.p, color = col, linewidth = 2.5, label = h)
end
scatter!(ax, ponds.canopy, Float64.(ponds.focal), color = (:grey40, 0.25))
axislegend(ax, position = :lt)

fig
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 9.5 — Predicting a new pond

A temporary pond has 80% canopy and water at 26 °C. According to `g4`, what is the
probability of finding the focal species there? Pass it to `check("9.5", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Build a one-row `DataFrame` with the columns `canopy`, `temp_c` and `hydro`, and pass
it to `predict(g4, ...)`, as with `grid` above.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-5
new_pond = DataFrame(canopy = [80.0], temp_c = [26.0], hydro = ["temporary"])
p_new = predict(g4, new_pond)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-5-check
check("9.5", p_new)
```

About 0.52. `predict` returns probabilities for a logistic GLM by default: the link
function is undone for you.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-9-5
#| include: false
Checks.verify("9.5", p_new)
```

## GLMMs {#sec-glmm}

```{julia}
#| label: glmm
gm1 = fit(MixedModel,
          @formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + (1 | region)),
          ponds, Poisson())
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

```r
glmer(richness ~ log_area + canopy + (1 | region),
      data = ponds, family = poisson)
```

The formula notation is the same, `(1 | group)` included. For the estimation method
used and the options available, consult the `MixedModels.jl` documentation
[@mixedmodelsjl]: these are details that change between versions, and not worth
reproducing here from memory.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 9.6 — A GLMM with hydroperiod

Add `hydro` to `gm1` and pass the fixed effects of the new model to
`check("9.6", ...)`. Compare the `hydro` estimate with the one from 9.1.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Add `+ hydro` before the random-effect term. `fixef(gm)` returns the fixed effects.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-6
gm_hydro = fit(MixedModel,
               @formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + hydro + (1 | region)),
               ponds, Poisson(); progress = false)
fixef(gm_hydro)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-9-6-check
check("9.6", fixef(gm_hydro))
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-9-6
#| include: false
Checks.verify("9.6", fixef(gm_hydro))
```

## Gaps you will hit {#sec-glm-gaps}

This is the point where being honest is worth more than being enthusiastic. The table
below is an assessment as of **August 2026**, made by checking the public package
registries; check before concluding that something does not exist.

| You need | In R | In Julia today |
|---|---|---|
| Zero-inflation, hurdle | `glmmTMB`, `pscl` | no mature equivalent |
| Beta regression | `betareg`, `glmmTMB` | no mature equivalent |
| Additive models (GAM) | `mgcv` | no mature equivalent |
| Simulated quantile residuals | `DHARMa` | none; implementable by hand |
| Marginal means, contrasts | `emmeans` | `Effects.jl`, partial coverage |
| Ordinal regression | `ordinal`, `MASS::polr` | partial coverage |

### The pragmatic escape hatch: `RCall.jl` {#sec-rcall}

There is no shame in calling R from inside Julia when the right package only exists
there. The workflow stays reproducible, and data crosses the boundary automatically.

```{julia}
#| label: rcall-example
#| eval: false
using RCall

@rput ponds        # send the DataFrame to R

R"""
library(mgcv)
m <- gam(richness ~ s(canopy) + s(log_area) + region,
         family = poisson, data = ponds)
summary(m)
"""
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this leaves you

For the repertoire covered by this chapter — Poisson, negative binomial, binomial,
gamma, offsets, GLMMs — Julia covers what you need, and this chapter has demonstrated
it with executed code. Outside it, `RCall.jl` is the bridge. Naming the boundary
clearly serves the reader better than hiding it.
:::

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

1. Compute the dispersion statistic for `g2`. Did the negative binomial fix the
   overdispersion? After 9.3, would you still choose it?
2. Build the predicted-probability curve of @fig-logistic for each hydroperiod at three
   temperatures (22, 24.5 and 27 °C). How much does temperature shift the curve?
3. Implement `DHARMa`-style quantile residuals for `g1`: simulate 250 datasets from the
   fitted model and, for each pond, compute the proportion of simulated values below
   the observed one. If the model is right, these proportions are uniform. Are they?
   Repeat for the model from 9.3.
